name: Default stance: AI not allowed
covers: The default rule bans generative AI on graded work (or on all work) in the course or unit.
name_v2: Prohibit AI on graded work by default

name: Default stance: AI allowed or encouraged
covers: The default rule allows, welcomes, encourages, or expects generative AI use.
name_v2: Permit or encourage AI by default

name: Default stance: AI discouraged but not banned
covers: AI is discouraged or not recommended, but not formally prohibited.
name_v2: Discourage AI without forbidding it

name: Instructor or assignment decides AI use
covers: Whether AI is allowed is decided per instructor, per assignment, or per activity rather than by one rule.
name_v2: Let each instructor or assignment set the rule

name: Named levels or tiers of AI use
covers: The policy defines named tiers, levels, colors, or categories of permitted AI use (e.g. no AI / limited / open), or a table of uses per assessment.
name_v2: Name explicit tiers or levels of AI use

name: Fallback rule when no AI rule is stated
covers: States what applies when a syllabus or assignment says nothing about AI (e.g. 'unless explicitly allowed, AI is prohibited').
name_v2: Define the fallback rule when a syllabus is silent

name: AI built into everyday tools (writing assistants, editors, IDEs, agents)
covers: Rules that cover AI built into editors and IDEs (Copilot, Cursor, autocomplete), operating systems, browsers, or autonomous coding agents, including requiring students to disable them.
name_v2: Cover AI built into editors, IDEs, and agents

name: AI permission staged as skills or work develop
covers: AI permission changes over the course: forbidden early, allowed later once fundamentals are mastered or in later projects or advanced courses.
name_v2: Stage AI permission as skills develop

name: AI rules stated in the syllabus and assignment instructions
covers: Instructors or departments must state AI expectations in the syllabus or assignment instructions.
name_v2: Require an AI statement in every syllabus

name: Asking when unsure about AI use
covers: Students who are unsure whether a use is allowed should ask the instructor first, or err on the side of not using AI.
name_v2: When unsure, students should ask before using AI

name: AI rules vary by course; permission does not carry over
covers: One course's AI permissions do not carry over to other courses or assignments.
name_v2: Each course's policy governs only that course

name: AI as a tutor for concepts and background
covers: AI may be used like a tutor or search engine to understand concepts, lecture material, or general questions, not to produce graded answers.
name_v2: Allow AI as a tutor for understanding concepts

name: AI for debugging and explaining errors
covers: AI may be used to explain error messages, help debug, or clarify syntax.
name_v2: Allow AI to explain errors and help debug

name: AI for study and practice (quizzes, flashcards, review)
covers: AI may be used to generate practice problems, study guides, summaries, reviews, or self-checks of knowledge.
name_v2: Allow AI for practice, study aids, and review

name: AI for brainstorming and early planning
covers: AI may be used for brainstorming, idea generation, or exploring alternative approaches.
name_v2: Allow AI for brainstorming and exploring approaches

name: AI-generated content or code in submitted work
covers: Students may submit or use AI-generated code under explicit conditions (small snippets, line or percentage caps, cited, specific projects, or freely).
name_v2: Allow AI-generated code under stated conditions

name: Course-specific or institution-provided AI tools
covers: The course or university provides its own sanctioned AI tool (a course chatbot, tutor bot, or licensed assistant), sometimes the only AI allowed.
name_v2: Provide a sanctioned, course-specific AI tool

name: Submitting AI-generated work as one's own
covers: Students may not submit work that AI produced as their own (the student submits AI output). P140 covers the outsourcing frame, where AI is one of the outside parties that may not do the work.
name_v2: Do not have AI produce the work you submit

name: Entering assignment questions or one's own work into AI
covers: Students may not paste or upload assignment specifications, questions, their own code, or the codebase into an AI tool.
name_v2: Do not feed assignment specs or your code to AI

name: AI for checking or debugging graded work
covers: Students may not use AI to debug, fix, proofread, reformat, or check graded work.
name_v2: Do not use AI to debug or check graded work

name: AI during exams, quizzes and in-class assessments
covers: No AI on exams, quizzes, tests, or in-class assessments; closed-device rules during exams.
name_v2: No AI on exams, quizzes, or in-class assessments

name: Keeping AI sessions separate from the submitted work
covers: Keep AI conversations separate from the work: close the AI before writing, never copy-paste from it, never have both open, or use only browser chat interfaces.
name_v2: Keep AI conversations apart from the work itself

name: Disclosing and acknowledging AI use
covers: Students must disclose, acknowledge, or cite any AI use in their submission (a statement or citation).
name_v2: Disclose AI use with each submission

name: What an AI citation or disclosure records (tool, prompt, output, format)
covers: Citations of AI must include specific details such as the tool or model, the exact prompt, the output, or the date.
name_v2: Cite the tool, the prompt, and the output

name: Process records: AI logs, drafts and reflections
covers: Students must keep and submit full transcripts, chat logs, journals, drafts, or reflections on their AI use.
name_v2: Keep and submit transcripts, logs, or reflections

name: Marking which parts of a submission are AI-derived
covers: AI-derived code must be marked at the exact place it is used (code comments, README, acknowledgments file, top of file).
name_v2: Mark AI-derived code where it is used

name: Nondisclosure as the violation
covers: How disclosure affects grading or integrity: disclosed use is not penalized, or failure to disclose is itself the violation (or, conversely, disclosed use is still penalized).
name_v2: Make disclosure safe and nondisclosure the violation

name: Submitted work must be one's own
covers: Students are responsible for and must own all work they submit; submitted work must be their own.
name_v2: Students own everything they submit

name: Explaining and defending one's own work
covers: Students must understand and be able to explain or defend every line and part of what they submit.
name_v2: Students must be able to explain every line

name: Verifying AI output
covers: AI output can be wrong, biased, or hallucinated; students must verify and critically evaluate it.
name_v2: Verify AI output; it is often wrong

name: AI supports, and does not replace, human thinking
covers: Students should remain the primary thinker and decision-maker; AI must not replace their thinking.
name_v2: Students stay the primary problem-solver

name: Supervised, proctored or in-class assessment
covers: Assessment weight shifts toward proctored, in-class, or unassisted evaluation because of AI.
name_v2: Shift weight to proctored, unassisted assessment

name: Explaining work orally (interviews, code reviews, presentations)
covers: Understanding is checked through code reviews, interviews, oral exams, demos, or meetings where students explain their work.
name_v2: Check understanding through code reviews, interviews, or oral exams

name: Assignment and assessment redesign for AI
covers: Assignments, grading schemes, or course structure are redesigned around AI (e.g. two-pass submissions, grading on process or hours, baselines for declared AI use). Includes assignment-specific AI interaction protocols, e.g. a required prompt header (UIUC CS 128).
name_v2: Redesign assignments and grading around AI

name: AI misuse as academic misconduct
covers: Unauthorized or improper AI use is classified as academic misconduct, plagiarism, or cheating and handled by integrity processes.
name_v2: Treat unauthorized AI use as academic misconduct

name: Consequences and sanctions for AI-rule violations
covers: Specific penalties for AI misuse are stated (zero, negative score, letter-grade reduction, course failure, escalation by offense).
name_v2: State concrete penalties in advance

name: Self-report, amnesty or leniency for inadvertent misuse
covers: Students can self-report, withdraw a submission, or come forward within a window for reduced consequences.
name_v2: Offer a self-report window or amnesty

name: Reliability and use of AI detectors
covers: AI detectors are unreliable or will not be used or relied upon as proof.
name_v2: Do not rely on AI detectors

name: Detection and similarity tools for AI misuse
covers: Similarity checking, plagiarism software, AI-detection tools, commit histories, or activity logs are used to identify misuse.
name_v2: Use similarity checks and process evidence instead

name: AI shortcuts the practice that builds skill
covers: AI use is limited because doing the work yourself builds skill; outsourcing practice undermines learning.
name_v2: Explain that AI shortcuts the practice that builds skill

name: Fundamentals before AI; protecting novices
covers: Beginners and foundational courses especially need to learn fundamentals without AI; novices cannot judge AI output.
name_v2: Protect novices; fundamentals come first

name: False sense of mastery from AI
covers: Relying on AI creates a false sense of mastery that is exposed on exams or later work.
name_v2: Warn that AI gives a false sense of mastery

name: Teaching AI use in courses
covers: Learning to use AI effectively is a professional skill employers expect; courses teach or demonstrate AI use.
name_v2: Teach effective AI use as a professional skill

name: AI under the existing rules for human help and sources
covers: AI is treated like a human collaborator, peer, or outside source under existing collaboration or citation rules. Distinct from P140: P45 applies existing rules for human help or sources to AI; P140 names AI among the parties that may not do a student's work.
name_v2: Treat AI like a human collaborator under existing rules

name: Human responsibility for grades
covers: Grades must be assigned by human instructors; AI will not grade or determine grades.
name_v2: Humans, not AI, assign grades

name: Instructor disclosure of their own AI and detector use
covers: Instructors disclose or describe their own use of AI (in grading, feedback, demos, or communication) to students, or commit to limits on it.
name_v2: Disclose instructor AI use to students

name: Disclosure and review of AI-made materials and communications
covers: Course materials created with AI are disclosed and reviewed by instructors.
name_v2: Review and disclose AI-made course materials

name: Uploading course materials and protected content to AI
covers: Students may not upload course materials, assignment descriptions, or protected works into AI tools.
name_v2: Do not upload course materials to AI tools

name: Keeping personal and sensitive data out of AI tools
covers: Protect personal and confidential data; AI tools store prompts; prefer university-vetted or licensed tools.
name_v2: Protect personal data and prefer vetted tools

name: Equitable access to AI (cost, alternatives, opt-out)
covers: Equity and access: AI is optional or not required, free access is provided, paid tools are not required, accommodations and alternatives exist.
name_v2: Do not require paid tools; keep access equitable

name: Copyright, intellectual property and terms of use
covers: Copyright, licensing, terms of use, and ownership of AI inputs and outputs.
name_v2: Consider licensing and copyright of AI output

name: Bias, fairness and general ethical concerns about AI
covers: Ethical, bias, labor, and environmental concerns about AI.
name_v2: Name bias, harms, and environmental costs

name: Policy review and revision over time
covers: The policy is provisional and will be revisited, revised, or updated; feedback is invited.
name_v2: Revisit the policy regularly

name: Evidence on AI use and its effects
covers: Evidence or data about how AI use affects student learning or performance is collected or cited.
name_v2: Gather evidence on how AI affects learning

name: Institutional values and principles for AI use
covers: An institution-level framework or preamble stating the purpose, scope, and principles for AI use.
name_v2: Set an institution-wide framework for responsible AI use

name: Instructor-student conversation before escalating suspected misuse
covers: Instructors should talk with the student and gather context before escalating suspected AI misuse.
name_v2: Talk with the student before escalating suspected misuse

name: Students' own course communication (posts, messages)
covers: Messages, emails or posts that students send to course staff must be written by the student, not generated by AI (source: UC Irvine ICS 33/H32).
name_v2: Students write their own course communication

name: Instructor AI use for teaching work
covers: What instructors or staff may, should or should not use AI for in their own teaching work: drafting syllabi, rubrics, quiz items, examples, feedback drafts, translations, letters. Final grading decisions are P46; disclosure to students is P47; AI-made course materials are P48 (sources: UIUC CITL and Grainger; Oregon State EECS).
name_v2: Instructor use of AI for teaching work

name: Trust and course design over policing AI use
covers: Staff state they will not actively police or detect AI use, relying instead on unassisted assessments or student responsibility (source: UIUC ECE 220).
name_v2: Decline to police AI use

name: Definitions and scope of the policy
covers: Definitions of AI, generative AI, AI tools or agentic systems that set what a policy covers (sources: Oregon State, Howard).
name_v2: Define AI and the policy's scope

name: AI in research, publication and review
covers: AI rules for theses, dissertations, manuscripts, grants and peer review, including deferring to venue, funder, sponsor or IRB rules (sources: Oregon State EECS, Howard Policy 100-022).
name_v2: Govern AI use in research and scholarship

name: Faculty support and learning about AI
covers: Workshops, consultations, faculty communities, and advice that instructors try AI tools and learn their implications before setting course policy (sources: Oregon State, Howard).
name_v2: Support faculty in learning AI

name: Due process for students accused of misuse
covers: Students accused of AI misuse have a right to respond or present evidence; fairness and transparency in AI-related integrity cases (source: Howard).
name_v2: Students may respond to AI-misuse allegations

name: Review and approval of AI tools and vendors
covers: Institutional review of AI contracts and partnerships, and limits on licensing or sharing university data and IP with AI providers (source: Howard Policy 100-022). Broadened 2026-10-26 (D33): also covers review and approval of any AI tool or system before purchase or deployment (security, risk, accessibility, legal), and periodic re-evaluation of approved tools. Evidence: Morehouse, Old Dominion, Rutgers (3), Santa Clara, Oakland, Penn State, Northwestern, Purdue.
name_v2: Review and approve AI tools, vendors and data sharing

name: Explaining and discussing AI rules with students
covers: Instructors give students the reasons behind their AI rules, discuss AI in class, or word the rules with care (tone, avoiding anthropomorphic language), going beyond listing the rule in the syllabus. Evidence before adding: Carleton, Brown, Boston College, Case Western, IU Indianapolis, Binghamton, George Mason, Michigan State.
name_v2: Explain and discuss the AI rules with students

name: Co-creating course AI policy with students
covers: Instructors set the course's AI expectations together with students, for example through class discussion, to build understanding and buy-in. Evidence: Cal Poly Pomona, Cal State LA, Georgetown, Georgia State.
name_v2: Co-create the AI policy with students

name: Educative response to misuse
covers: Treat suspected or confirmed AI misuse, especially first offenses, as a learning opportunity; prefer educative or remedial responses; presume good faith; reduce the pressures that lead to cheating. Different from P60 (declining to police) and P57 (talking before escalating). Evidence: Austin CC, East Tennessee State, Florida State, IU Indianapolis, George Washington, Clemson, Case Western.
name_v2: Respond to misuse educatively, not only punitively

name: Evidence standards for AI-misuse findings
covers: What evidence is needed, or not sufficient, to find AI misuse: a standard of proof, the kinds of evidence to weigh, or the statement that a hunch that work 'does not sound like the student' is not enough. Evidence: Cornell, Grinnell, Iowa State, Clark, Georgetown. Broadened 2026-10-26 (D33): also covers rules that detector output may be used only as supporting evidence, not as proof. Evidence: Oberlin, Rice, Santa Clara, Old Dominion, Rowan.
name_v2: Set evidence standards for AI-misuse findings

name: AI literacy training and resources
covers: The institution offers or mandates AI-literacy training, modules, guides or curricular AI-literacy for students, staff or the whole community. Faculty-only support is P63. Evidence: Georgia Southern, Kennesaw State, Clark, East Tennessee State, Florida International, Brown, Baylor, Cleveland State.
name_v2: Provide or require AI training for students and staff

name: Reporting AI incidents and misuse
covers: A duty or channel to report AI-related problems: accidental exposure of sensitive data, tool malfunctions, policy violations or misconduct by others. Evidence: Augusta, Case Western, Georgia State, Kansas State, Marquette.
name_v2: Report AI incidents, data exposure and misuse

name: Contact points and human help for AI questions
covers: Students are directed to instructors, librarians, writing centers, advisors or other human support, alongside or instead of AI tools. Evidence: Marquette, Harvey Mudd, Cal State, Florida International, BYU, Clemson.
name_v2: Point students to human help alongside AI

name: Human oversight of AI-influenced decisions
covers: AI may not be the sole basis for consequential decisions about individuals, such as hiring, admissions, discipline, evaluation or academic standing; a human reviews and decides. Grading alone is P46. Evidence: Austin CC, Clark, Colby, Hampton, Michigan State.
name_v2: Keep humans responsible for decisions about people

name: Harmful, deceptive or fabricating AI uses
covers: General conduct rules against using AI to deceive, impersonate, fabricate or falsify data or records, harass, spread misinformation, write malware or breach security. Evidence: Cal State, East Tennessee State, George Mason, Kansas State, LSU, Michigan State, Colby.
name_v2: Ban deceptive, fabricated or malicious AI use

name: AI-enabled phishing and security threats
covers: Security awareness: watch for AI-crafted phishing, scams and deepfakes, and report suspicious messages. Evidence: Bowdoin, Bucknell, Colby, East Carolina, Georgia Tech, Howard, Lamar.
name_v2: Guard against AI-enabled phishing and security threats

name: Administrative and operational AI use
covers: Rules for AI in university operations outside teaching, such as staff administrative work, student services, official communications, chatbots or AI-built apps shared with others. Evidence: Brandeis, Hampton, Davidson, Kansas State, DePaul, Cal State.
name_v2: Govern administrative and operational AI use

name: Existing law and university policy apply to AI
covers: AI use must follow laws (records, privacy, IP) and existing university policies (conduct, acceptable use, branding), and violations fall under those policies. Different from P45, which treats AI like a human collaborator under integrity rules. Evidence: Amherst, Boise State, Kansas State, Arizona State, Cal State, Davidson.
name_v2: Comply with existing law and university policy

name: Finding out and following each course's AI rules
covers: Students are responsible for finding out, reading and following the AI rules that apply to them in each course, program or assignment (check the syllabus first). Different from P10 (ask when unsure) and P11 (a course's rule binds only that course). Evidence: Georgetown, Harvey Mudd, Rutgers-Camden, Rutgers-Newark, Princeton, Oakland, San José State, NIU, Northwestern, NAU, Portland State.
name_v2: Students learn and follow each course's AI rules

name: AI use built into coursework
covers: AI use is built into, expected in or required for an assignment or course, or instructors are told they may require it. Evidence: Ohio State, RIT, Brown, Oregon State, Pepperdine, Oakland, Northeastern, Sam Houston State.
name_v2: Require AI use in some coursework

name: Governance roles, ownership and exceptions
covers: Names the office, officer, council or committee that interprets, implements, monitors or enforces the AI policy, or the process for granting exceptions to it. Evidence: Purdue, Rowan, Oakland, Morehouse, Northeastern, Northwestern, Portland State, Santa Clara.
name_v2: Name who owns, enforces and grants exceptions to the AI policy

name: Formal integrity procedure (reporting, referral, sanctions process)
covers: Procedural steps once misuse is suspected or sanctioned: instructors file a report with a central office, meet deadlines, use a required form, and leave sanctions to the deciding body. Different from P36 (classifying misuse as misconduct) and P57 (talking with the student first). Evidence: San José State, RPI, Rowan, SMU, Santa Clara, Oregon State, Rice, Oberlin, Portland State.
name_v2: Follow the formal integrity-reporting procedure

name: Limits of preventing and detecting AI use
covers: States limits on control: bans are impractical or counterproductive, AI use cannot be fully eliminated, faculty cannot always verify originality, assessments lose reliability. Evidence: Rush, NC A&T, Oregon State, RIT, MIT, NC State.
name_v2: Acknowledge that AI use cannot be fully prevented or verified

name: AI decisions grounded in learning objectives
covers: Whether and how AI is allowed should follow from the course's or program's learning objectives. Evidence: Rush, Northeastern, Case Western, SF State, Morehouse, Santa Clara, Middle Tennessee State.
name_v2: Align AI decisions with learning objectives

name: How the policy was made (body, process, sources, AI assistance)
covers: States the process, body or date by which the AI policy or guidance was drafted, consulted on, adopted or ratified. Evidence: New Mexico State, Rice, Northeastern, Santa Clara.
name_v2: Describe how and by whom the policy was made

name: Units set their own AI rules
covers: Colleges, schools, departments or programs may set their own or additional AI rules, or have different expectations from the university-wide rule. P04 is the instructor-level version. Evidence: Santa Clara, Saint Louis, Northeastern, San Diego State, Purdue, Middle Tennessee State, SMU.
name_v2: Let schools or units set their own AI rules

name: Consent for AI recording, transcription and likeness
covers: Class sessions or meetings may not be recorded or transcribed by AI tools without permission or announcement. Evidence: Augusta, Kean, Oregon State, Santa Clara.
name_v2: Require consent before AI recording or transcription

name: Benefits of AI for learning and teaching
covers: Names benefits of AI for teaching and learning (personalization, accessibility, efficiency, creativity) without making it a rule or a career-skill claim (P44). Evidence: New Mexico State, LSU, Ohio State, NC State, Prairie View A&M, Rush, SF State.
name_v2: State the benefits of AI for learning

name: Engaging peers, partners and the community on AI
covers: Coalitions with other universities, benchmarking against peers, partnerships with industry or government, and public forums on AI. Evidence: Brown, EVMS, Kansas State, Old Dominion.
name_v2: Engage peers, partners and the community on AI

name: AI for data analysis and visualization
covers: AI may be used to analyze, sort, simulate or visualize data. Evidence: Ohio State, Morehouse, FIU, SMU, NAU, Sam Houston State.
name_v2: Allow AI for data analysis and visualization

name: Own attempt first, then AI
covers: A sequencing rule: the student first attempts, drafts or develops the work without AI, and AI help is allowed only afterward. Evidence: Ohio State, North Dakota State, Oregon State, Northwestern.
name_v2: Do the work yourself first, then use AI

name: AI for editing, proofreading and outlining one's own work
covers: AI may help with editing, proofreading, grammar, outlining, organizing or revising one's own writing. P18 is about treating prose differently from code; this is the permission itself. Evidence: Morehouse, Rutgers, NAU, Ohio State, Oakland, Rowan, Penn State, Rush, NC State.
name_v2: Allow AI for editing, proofreading and writing support

name: University-licensed or approved AI tools
covers: Use the AI tools the university licenses, provides or approves (institution-wide, not one course: that is P17), or know the approved list. Evidence: NYU, Morehouse, Rutgers (3 campuses), SUNY ESF, RIT, Nova Southeastern, Rowan, NC State.
name_v2: Use university-licensed or approved AI tools

name: Prompting advice
covers: Practical advice on writing prompts or probing AI tools to get better results or learn their limits. Evidence: Pepperdine, Oakland, Sam Houston State, Santa Clara, San Diego State, NC State.
name_v2: Advise on how to prompt AI effectively

name: Careers and professional norms as reasons to build skills without AI
covers: The reason given for limiting AI is professional readiness: employers expect skills, critical thinking or work in settings without AI. P44 is the opposite argument (learn AI for careers). Evidence: Oregon State, RIT, Santa Clara, Princeton.
name_v2: Cite careers as a reason to build skills without AI

name: Integrity, honesty and fairness as grounds for AI rules
covers: The reason given for AI rules is fairness to other students, honest evaluation, or the integrity culture of the community, not skill-building (P41). Evidence: CUNY Graduate Center, Santa Clara, Prairie View A&M, Northeastern Illinois, San José State, Oberlin.
name_v2: Ground AI limits in fairness and academic honesty

name: AI is not an author, source or collaborator
covers: AI is not a person: it cannot be an author, a cited source or a group member, and AI use is not acceptable collaboration. The opposite of P45. Evidence: Princeton, Pepperdine, Santa Clara.
name_v2: Treat AI as neither author, source nor collaborator

name: Accessibility and AI
covers: Accessibility of AI tools and AI-produced materials for people with disabilities: accessibility reviews, alternative access plans, accessible output, AI as an accessibility aid. P51 covers cost and equal access. Evidence: Nova Southeastern, Ohio State, Penn State, Oregon State, Santa Clara, NAU.
name_v2: Make AI use and output accessible

name: Documenting, auditing and monitoring AI systems
covers: Institutional AI systems are documented (model cards, records), audited or monitored for bias, accuracy, security and drift over time. Evidence: Morehouse, Georgia Southern, Old Dominion, Saint Louis, Oakland, Northwestern.
name_v2: Document, audit and monitor deployed AI systems

name: Reducing pressures that lead to misuse
covers: Prevention by easing the causes of misuse: extensions, office hours, support resources, time management, explaining assignment purposes. P68 is the response after misuse. Evidence: Clemson, Rice, Old Dominion, IU Indianapolis, BYU.
name_v2: Reduce the pressures that lead to AI misuse

name: Routine or minor AI uses outside the rules
covers: Routine embedded features (spell-check, grammar check, search, autocomplete) are allowed or need no disclosure even under a restrictive rule. Evidence: Oregon State, Morehouse, Pepperdine.
name_v2: Exempt routine AI features from the rules

name: AI in grading and feedback by instructors
covers: AI-assisted grading or feedback is allowed only under conditions: approval chains, explainability, human review of AI-drafted feedback, closed-form only. P46 is the rule that only humans assign grades. Evidence: Penn State, Purdue, Northeastern, SMU, Old Dominion, Oregon State.
name_v2: Set conditions for AI-assisted grading

name: Staying informed about AI developments
covers: A duty or encouragement for users to keep up with AI developments, best practices and the institution's current AI guidance. Evidence: East Tennessee State, San Diego State, NAU.
name_v2: Stay informed about AI developments and guidance

name: Notice when AI is used in interactions or decisions
covers: People have a right to know when they are dealing with an AI system (chatbots, deployed systems), including its scope and limits. P47 is instructor disclosure to students. Evidence: Northwestern, Cal State, Morehouse.
name_v2: Tell people when they are interacting with AI

name: AI for literature search and finding sources
covers: AI may help find, screen or annotate sources and literature, usually on condition that the student reads and verifies them. Evidence: idaho, rowan, tennessee-state, new-school, tulane.
name_v2: Allow AI for literature search and finding sources

name: AI for reading and summarizing sources
covers: Students may not use AI to summarize, contextualize or digest assigned readings or source material, even when no AI output is submitted (a ban on study use, the opposite of P14). Evidence: arizona, nevada-reno, texas-christian, brandeis.
name_v2: Ban AI for reading and summarizing sources

name: AI for images and multimedia
covers: AI may generate figures, illustrations, storyboards or graphics, often only if they contain no data. Evidence: rowan, stony-brook, alabama-huntsville, nebraska-lincoln, louisiana-lafayette.
name_v2: Allow AI for images and illustrations

name: Prior approval or a closed list of permitted uses
covers: AI is allowed only after explicit prior approval (sometimes a written proposal of the intended use) or only for a closed list of tasks. P10 is asking when unsure; P05 names tiers. Evidence: seton-hall, teachers-college-columbia, vermont, unc-charlotte, texas-health-science-center-houston.
name_v2: Require prior approval or limit AI to listed tasks

name: No institution-wide AI policy exists
covers: The document says the institution (or its integrity policy) has no AI-specific or uniform policy, often as the reason decisions fall to instructors. Evidence: william-and-mary, nevada-las-vegas, central-florida, seton-hall, maryland-baltimore-county.
name_v2: State that no specific AI policy exists

name: Aligning AI rules across sections, departments and disciplines
covers: Instructors should align AI rules and penalties with colleagues, across sections of one course, or with their discipline's norms, so students meet consistent rules. P85 is units setting their own rules. Evidence: temple, kansas, louisville, delaware, california-riverside, colorado-state, northeastern.
name_v2: Coordinate AI rules across sections, departments and disciplines

name: Sample syllabus language and templates
covers: The institution supplies sample AI syllabus statements or templates for instructors to adopt. P63 is helping faculty learn about AI. Evidence: maryland-baltimore-county, tennessee-technological, maryland-baltimore.
name_v2: Provide sample syllabus language and templates

name: Integrity pledges and signed AI agreements
covers: Students sign or reaffirm an honor code, integrity pledge or AI-use agreement, per course, per assessment or per term. Evidence: seton-hall, delaware, california-santa-cruz, california-san-diego, syracuse, florida-international.
name_v2: Have students sign an integrity pledge or AI agreement

name: Instructors modeling responsible AI use
covers: Instructors' own AI use and mentorship are framed as teaching responsible use by example. P59 is instructor AI use for teaching work. Evidence: william-and-mary, texas-tech, texas-aandm.
name_v2: Instructors model responsible AI use

name: Institutional monitoring of AI use
covers: The institution may access, review or audit prompts, outputs and accounts on its AI tools; users have no expectation of privacy there. Evidence: maryland-college-park, maryland-baltimore, nevada-reno.
name_v2: Reserve the right to monitor AI use

name: Personal responsibility for self-chosen AI tools
covers: People who accept an AI tool's terms or use unlicensed tools on their own carry the risk and liability; the institution disclaims guarantees. Evidence: maryland-college-park, maryland-baltimore, texas-medical-branch-galveston, nevada-reno, louisville.
name_v2: Users bear responsibility for AI tools they sign up for

name: Pointers to further AI guidance and resources
covers: The document directs readers to other pages, guides or offices for AI rules, citation formats or support. P72 is human help for students. Evidence: tennessee-technological, ohio-state, arkansas, dayton.
name_v2: Point to further AI guidance and resources

name: General expectation of ethical, responsible use
covers: A general call to use AI ethically and responsibly with no specific content; kept so such statements are counted but not overread. Evidence: texas-dallas, massachusetts-boston, south-florida, minnesota, southern.
name_v2: State a general expectation of ethical, responsible use

name: Evaluating an AI tool before choosing it
covers: Users should research, test or assess a tool (accuracy, trustworthiness, fit to the task) before choosing it. P65 is institutional review and approval. Evidence: swarthmore-college, colorado-colorado-springs, seattle, colorado-boulder, northeastern.
name_v2: Evaluate an AI tool and choose one suited to the task

name: Weighing benefits and risks before using AI
covers: Users decide whether to use AI by weighing its gains, risks, ethics and their own values in context. Evidence: maryland-baltimore, seton-hall, alaska-fairbanks, colorado-boulder, unc-charlotte, tulane, nevada-las-vegas.
name_v2: Weigh benefits, risks and values before using AI

name: AI for career and personal tasks outside coursework
covers: AI suggested or allowed for job preparation, career planning or everyday personal tasks, sometimes with a note to check employers' rules. Evidence: tennessee-state, syracuse, central-florida, swarthmore-college.
name_v2: Allow AI for career and personal tasks outside coursework

name: Fabricated citations and unattributed sources in AI output
covers: AI reproduces sources without attribution, so using its output risks unintentional plagiarism or fabrication. Evidence: new-school, colorado-boulder, massachusetts-lowell.
name_v2: Warn that AI output can cause unintentional plagiarism

name: AI displacing human interaction and feedback
covers: Overreliance on AI can reduce contact with instructors and peers or replace human feedback that learning depends on. Evidence: cornell, alabama-birmingham, texas-austin.
name_v2: Warn that AI can displace human interaction and feedback

name: Institutional investment in AI capacity
covers: Institutional commitments to AI research centers, computing resources, funding or collaboration; not rules on AI use. Evidence: tennessee-technological, louisville, william-and-mary, tulane, arkansas-little-rock.
name_v2: Invest in AI research, infrastructure and capacity

name: Telling students how misuse will be detected and handled
covers: Course policies should state how AI misuse will be detected and how it will be handled. P36 classes misuse as misconduct; P37 states penalties. Evidence: kansas, nevada-las-vegas, uc-irvine, purdue, santa-clara.
name_v2: Say how misuse will be detected and handled

name: Consistent and transparent application of AI rules
covers: Instructors apply their AI expectations the same way to all students and make them transparent. Evidence: uc-irvine, middle-tennessee-state, boston.
name_v2: Apply AI rules consistently and transparently

name: Students checking their own work for similarity or AI
covers: Students are offered or pointed to tools to check their own drafts for similarity or AI-generated text before submitting. Evidence: arkansas-little-rock, boston, oregon-state.
name_v2: Let students check their own work for similarity or AI

name: Security of AI accounts, systems and AI-written code
covers: Security controls for AI accounts and systems: multi-factor authentication, credentials, patching, access limits and controls on AI agents. P75 is AI-enabled threats. Evidence: texas-san-antonio, ut-rio-grande-valley, houston, morehouse-college.
name_v2: Secure AI accounts and systems

name: AI in group work
covers: Rules for AI use in group projects: members agree on use, say what to do if one member uses AI, or share responsibility for a violation. Evidence: washington, arizona-state, north-carolina-state.
name_v2: Set AI rules for group work

name: AI for translation and language support
covers: Rules on using AI to translate text or to support language learning (permitted, conditioned or banned). Split out of P18 and from reviewer NEW labels.

name: AI feedback or critique on one's own work
covers: Using AI to get feedback, critique or review of one's own draft, code or solution (not to produce it). From P14, P91 subgroups and NEW labels.

name: Signs and indicators of AI-written work
covers: Manual signs, comparisons and indicators instructors use to suspect AI-written work (style shifts, fabricated citations, comparison with earlier work), as distinct from detector tools (P40) and standards of proof (P69).

name: What AI can and cannot do (capabilities and limits)
covers: Statements about AI's capabilities and limits beyond wrong output (P31): low quality, shallow reasoning, changing capability, what tools are and are not good for.

name: Status of the guidance (advisory or binding, precedence)
covers: The document says whether it is guidance or binding policy, and which text prevails when guidance and formal policy conflict.

name: Accountability for AI-assisted output
covers: Users are responsible for the accuracy, quality and consequences of AI-assisted work they submit or use (split from P29, which keeps 'submitted work must be one's own').

name: Career and workplace readiness as a reason to learn AI
covers: Preparing students for an AI-shaped workplace as the rationale for teaching or allowing AI (split from P44, which keeps teaching AI use in courses).

name: Environmental cost of AI
covers: Energy, water and carbon costs of AI named as a concern (split from P53).

name: Labor, consent and credit behind AI
covers: Concerns about uncredited labor, training on work without consent, and exploitation in building AI (split from P53).

name: AI records retention and public-records duties
covers: AI prompts, outputs and logs as records subject to retention rules or public-records requests.

name: AI is widespread and here to stay
covers: Context statements that AI is inevitable, already widespread or here to stay, used to frame the policy.

name: Purpose and context of the policy document
covers: Why the document exists, what problem it addresses and its context (split from P56, which keeps values and principles).

name: Having another person or AI do your course work
covers: Outsourcing: students may not have another person, entity, service or AI do their work for a course (the outside party does the work, as in contract cheating). Split from P19 on PI review (D58).
